"Buxom" is an adjective used to describe a woman who has a full, rounded, and voluptuous body — especially a large, prominent bust (chest). Think of a woman who is plump and curvy in a way that looks healthy, lively, and physically robust. It is not just about being heavy or overweight; it specifically points to a kind of attractive fullness, a figure that is round and well-developed rather than thin or flat.

The word puts the strongest spotlight on a woman's chest — a notably large bust is the feature most closely tied to "buxom." But the word doesn't stop there. It also suggests an overall generous, curvaceous figure: full hips, a rounded body, rosy cheeks — a woman who looks physically abundant and hearty rather than slim and angular. In short, if you picture a woman who is big-chested, curvy, and radiates physical vitality, that is a buxom woman.
Tone and connotation — is it a compliment?

Yes, traditionally it is complimentary. The word carries warm, positive overtones. It doesn't suggest someone is unhealthily fat or unattractive. On the contrary, it implies a kind of appealing, earthy, robust beauty — a woman who looks full of life and energy.

However, the word has an old-fashioned, slightly quaint flavor. You are more likely to find it in historical novels, period films, or classic literature than in everyday modern conversation. If someone used it today, it would likely sound a little literary or dated — not rude, but not current either.
Strictly women. You would almost never describe a man as "buxom." It is a word tied entirely to female physical appearance.

• It does not simply mean "fat" or "obese." Those words suggest excessive weight without the implication of attractiveness. "Buxom" implies a pleasing, voluptuous fullness.
  • It does not describe someone's personality, behavior, or character.
  • It does not mean tall or short — it is purely about body shape and build.
  • It does not carry the clinical coldness of words like "overweight." It is descriptive and appreciative.
Where and how is it used?

You will most commonly encounter "buxom" in:

  • Historical fiction and romance novels — "The buxom innkeeper greeted them with a broad smile."
  • Descriptions of classical paintings or sculptures — "The buxom figures in Rubens' paintings were considered the ideal of beauty in his era."
  • Period dramas and fairy tales — "A buxom milkmaid carried two pails across the yard."
  • Casual, slightly playful descriptions — "She was a cheerful, buxom woman who made everyone feel at home."

If it helps, picture the women painted by Peter Paul Rubens (the 17th-century Flemish painter) — full-figured, round, large-bosomed, glowing with health. Those women are the very picture of "buxom." The word almost always brings to mind something warm, lush, and generously proportioned, not gaunt, not delicate.
Buxom describes a woman with a notably large bust and a full, curvaceous, healthy-looking figure — used as a compliment, though it has an old-fashioned ring to it.
